question: Which description best matches a system of particles in mechanics?
opt_a: A rigid body restricted to rotational motion only
opt_b: A single particle chosen for point-mass analysis
opt_c: A point fixed permanently at the origin
opt_d: A collection of particles studied together
explanation: A system of particles means a group of particles considered as one chosen system. The particles may interact with one another, and forces from outside the system may also act on them. This idea lets us describe the motion of many-particle bodies without following every particle separately in every situation. For translational motion, the centre of mass often represents the system in a compact way. A single-particle model is only a special simpler case, while a system can contain many particles with different positions and velocities.

question: A rigid body is best idealised as a body in which
opt_a: all particles move only along straight paths
opt_b: distances between particle pairs remain fixed
opt_c: the body has zero mass and zero size
opt_d: every particle remains fixed at one position
explanation: A rigid body is an ideal body whose shape and size do not change during motion. This means the separation between any two particles of the body remains fixed. The body as a whole may translate, rotate, or do both, but its internal geometry is treated as unchanged. Real bodies can deform slightly, yet the rigid-body approximation works well when the deformation is too small to affect the motion being studied. Rigidity is about fixed relative distances, not about the body being motionless.

question: A block sliding on a smooth horizontal table without turning is an example mainly of
opt_a: circular motion of every particle about the same axis
opt_b: pure rotational motion about its centre
opt_d: pure translational motion
explanation: In pure translational motion, all particles of the body have the same displacement during the same time interval. A sliding block that does not turn keeps its orientation unchanged while every point shifts in the same direction. No point of the block is revolving around an axis of the block. Rotation would require the body to change its orientation or for its particles to move in circles around an axis. The key feature here is common displacement of all points, not the shape of the path alone.

question: Which idea is closest to the basic meaning of centre of mass?
opt_a: A mass-weighted representative point for translational motion
opt_b: The point that must always lie inside the material of the body
opt_c: The point where all external forces must always act
opt_d: The geometrical centre of every body
explanation: The centre of mass is a representative point whose position depends on how mass is distributed in a system. It is called mass-weighted because heavier parts influence its position more strongly than lighter parts. For many purposes, the translational motion of a system can be described as the motion of its centre of mass. It is not necessarily the same as the geometrical centre unless the body has suitable uniformity and symmetry. The centre of mass may even lie at a point where no material is present, such as the centre of a uniform ring.

question: In rotational motion about a fixed axis, the particles of a rigid body generally
opt_a: remain at the same point in space
opt_b: move with no relation to one another
opt_c: move in circles whose centres lie on the axis
opt_d: lose their fixed separation from neighbouring particles
explanation: When a rigid body rotates about a fixed axis, each particle not lying on the axis follows a circular path. The centre of that circular path lies on the axis of rotation. Particles at different distances from the axis trace circles of different radii. The body remains rigid because the relative distances between its particles do not change during this motion. Rotation is identified by change of orientation about an axis, not by the body simply shifting from one place to another.

question:
Match the basic quantity or symbol with its usual meaning.
Column IColumn II
P. \(\vec{r}\)1. Position vector of a particle
Q. \(M\)2. Total mass of the system
R. \(\vec{v}_{\text{CM}}\)3. Velocity of the centre of mass
S. \(\vec{\omega}\)4. Angular velocity
explanation: The symbol \(\vec{r}\) commonly represents the position vector of a particle measured from a chosen origin. The symbol \(M\) is used for the total mass of a system, especially when many particles are being treated together. The notation \(\vec{v}_{\text{CM}}\) represents the velocity of the centre of mass. The vector \(\vec{\omega}\) represents angular velocity, whose direction is associated with the axis of rotation. The vector arrow matters for quantities such as \(\vec{r}\), \(\vec{v}_{\text{CM}}\), and \(\vec{\omega}\), while \(M\) is a scalar mass.

question: The coordinate of the centre of mass is a position coordinate, so its SI unit is
opt_d: \(\text{m}\)
explanation: A centre-of-mass coordinate tells where the centre of mass is located along an axis. Since it is a position coordinate, it has the same unit as length. In SI, length is measured in \(\text{m}\). The unit \(\text{kg}\) belongs to mass, \(\text{s}\) belongs to time, and \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\) belongs to angular velocity. The centre of mass may depend on masses, but its coordinate still measures position.

question:
Study the row entries and identify the fully suitable pairing.
RowQuantityUsual unit
PTotal mass \(M\)\(\text{kg}\)
QTime \(t\)\(\text{m}\)
RAngular velocity \(\omega\)\(\text{N m}\)
SPosition coordinate \(x\)\(\text{rad s}^{-1}\)
opt_d: Row P
explanation: The total mass \(M\) of a system is measured in \(\text{kg}\), so row P gives a suitable pairing. Time \(t\) is measured in \(\text{s}\), not in \(\text{m}\). Angular velocity \(\omega\) is measured in \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\), while \(\text{N m}\) is the unit of torque. A position coordinate such as \(x\) is measured in \(\text{m}\), not in \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\). Unit matching is useful because it separates position, mass, time, rotation rate, and turning effect.

question:
Consider the following statements about the particle model and the rigid-body model.
I. A particle model ignores the size and shape of the body.
II. A rigid-body model allows rotation while keeping relative distances fixed.
III. A rigid body must always be treated as a single point.
opt_d: I, II, and III
explanation: A particle model treats a body as if its size and shape are not important for the question being studied. A rigid-body model keeps the size and shape important, but assumes the body does not deform. Such a body can translate, rotate, or perform a combination of both motions. Statement III is not suitable because a rigid body is extended and need not be reduced to a single point for rotational study. The particle model is useful for pure translation, while the rigid-body model is needed when orientation and rotation matter.

question: A rotating ceiling fan is considered a rigid body in elementary rotational motion because
opt_a: its mass becomes zero during rotation
opt_b: the blades keep fixed shape while rotating
opt_c: all blade points have the same linear speed
opt_d: its axis of rotation is absent
explanation: A ceiling fan is treated as a rigid body when the distances between particles of its blades are assumed to remain unchanged. The blades rotate about a fixed axis, but their shape is not considered to deform appreciably. Points at different distances from the axis generally have different linear speeds, so equal linear speed does not describe rigid-body behaviour. The fan certainly has an axis of rotation passing through its centre. The rigid-body approximation lets us study rotation without tracking small elastic bending of the blades.

question: A wheel rolls forward on a horizontal road without slipping. At the simplest classification level, its motion is a combination of
opt_a: rotation only, with no forward motion
opt_c: translation of its centre with rotation about it
opt_d: deformation of the wheel with no regular rolling
explanation: A rolling wheel moves forward as a whole, so its centre has translational motion. At the same time, the wheel turns about its central axis, so it also has rotational motion. This combination is different from a block sliding without turning, which is mainly translational. It is also different from a wheel spinning in place, where the centre does not move forward. Rolling motion becomes clearer only when both translation of the centre and rotation about the centre are kept together.

question: The total mass symbol \(M\) for a system of particles represents
opt_a: the mass of only the fastest particle
opt_b: the sum of all particle masses in the system
opt_c: the algebraic sum of position coordinates
opt_d: the distance of the centre of mass from the origin
explanation: For a system of particles, \(M\) denotes the total mass included in the chosen system. If the particles have masses \(m_1\), \(m_2\), \(m_3\), and so on, then \(M=m_1+m_2+m_3+\cdots\). This is not a position coordinate and does not depend on which particle is moving fastest. The system boundary decides which particles are included in \(M\). This notation is important because centre-of-mass formulas divide the mass-weighted position sum by the total mass.

question: For three particles of masses \(2\,\text{kg}\), \(3\,\text{kg}\), and \(5\,\text{kg}\) included in one system, what is the total mass \(M\)?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given masses:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(m_2=3\,\text{kg}\), and \(m_3=5\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Total mass \(M\) of the chosen system.
\( \textbf{Relevant relation:} \)
\[
M=m_1+m_2+m_3
\]
\( \textbf{Why this relation applies:} \) Total mass is found by adding the masses of all particles included in the system.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
M=2\,\text{kg}+3\,\text{kg}+5\,\text{kg}
\]
\( \textbf{Addition:} \)
\[
M=10\,\text{kg}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit check:} \) Each term is a mass in \(\text{kg}\), so the final unit remains \(\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The total mass of the system is \(10\,\text{kg}\).

question: Use the arrangement described below. Two unequal masses are placed on a light horizontal line, with the heavier mass on the right and the lighter mass on the left. Without calculating, the centre of mass of the two-mass system will lie
opt_a: exactly midway between the two masses
opt_d: outside the line segment on the lighter side
explanation: The centre of mass is a mass-weighted position, so the heavier mass has a stronger influence on its location. For two masses placed on a line, the centre of mass lies somewhere between them if both masses are positive and separated. It is exactly at the midpoint only when the two masses are equal. Since the right mass is heavier here, the representative point shifts toward the right side. This gives the physical meaning before using the formula \(X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}\).

question: The expression \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}\) most naturally denotes
opt_a: the radius vector of a circular path only
opt_b: the rotational kinetic energy of a body
opt_c: the position vector of the centre of mass
opt_d: the torque acting on the chosen system
explanation: The symbol \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}\) is commonly used for the position vector of the centre of mass of a system. The subscript \(\text{CM}\) indicates that the quantity belongs to the centre of mass. The vector arrow shows that position has both magnitude and direction relative to a chosen origin. Rotational kinetic energy is usually written as \(K_{\text{rot}}\), while torque is represented by \(\vec{\tau}\). The notation \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}\) is a system-level position, not simply the radius of one particle’s circular path.

question: A body moves so that every line drawn inside it remains parallel to its initial direction throughout the motion. This observation mainly indicates
opt_b: change in shape due to deformation
opt_d: translational motion
explanation: If every line in a body remains parallel to its original direction, the body is not changing its orientation. That is the signature of translational motion. The body may move along a straight or curved path, but all its particles have equal displacement during the same time interval in pure translation. Rotation would make internal lines turn through an angle, changing their direction in space. Translation is about common displacement of all points, not about the body necessarily moving with constant velocity.

question: In the notation used for rotational motion, \(I\) is introduced as the symbol for
opt_d: angular displacement
explanation: The symbol \(I\) denotes moment of inertia in rotational motion. It is the rotational analogue of mass in the sense that it measures resistance to angular acceleration about a specified axis. Unlike mass, \(I\) depends on how mass is distributed relative to the chosen axis. Its SI unit is \(\text{kg m}^2\), which already shows that both mass and distance from the axis are involved. This symbol is central in rotational dynamics and rotational kinetic energy.

question: A rotating door, a spinning wheel, and a balanced beam are useful early examples because all of them involve
opt_a: point-particle motion where body size has no role
opt_b: systems on which forces cannot act
opt_c: extended bodies where turning effects matter
opt_d: bodies whose total mass must be zero
explanation: These examples cannot be fully described by treating the body as a single point in every situation. A rotating door has an axis near its hinge, a spinning wheel rotates about its axle, and a balanced beam depends on how forces act at different positions. Their size, shape, and orientation are relevant to the motion or balance. Such examples motivate the need for rigid-body ideas after single-particle mechanics. They also show why quantities such as torque, angular velocity, and moment of inertia are needed for extended bodies.

question: A system boundary is chosen around two carts connected by a compressed spring. If both carts are included in the system, the spring forces between the carts are classified as
opt_a: internal forces between parts of the system
opt_b: rotational forces because the carts separate
opt_c: external forces because they change speeds
opt_d: zero forces because springs cannot act inside
explanation: A force is called internal or external only after the system has been chosen. When both carts are included in the same system, the spring force exerted by one cart on the other is a force between parts of that system. Such forces may change the motion of individual particles or bodies inside the system, but they are still internal forces for the system as a whole. If one cart alone were chosen as the system, the spring force on that cart would be external. The classification depends on the chosen boundary, not on whether the force is large or small.

question: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a circle. If the chosen system is only the stone, the tension exerted by the string on the stone is
opt_c: absent because the motion is circular
opt_d: a force that must be ignored in system analysis
explanation: The chosen system here contains only the stone. The string is outside that chosen system, so the force exerted by the string on the stone comes from outside the system. Therefore, the tension is an external force for the stone-only system. If the system were redefined to include both stone and string, the classification of some interactions would change. Internal and external are system-dependent labels, so the boundary must be fixed before classifying forces.

question: In a rigid-body approximation, a metal rod can translate and rotate, but it is assumed that
opt_a: no force can act on it
opt_b: its centre of mass must remain fixed
opt_c: every point must have the same velocity at every instant
opt_d: its particles keep fixed relative separations
explanation: A rigid-body approximation keeps the shape and size of the body unchanged. This means the distance between any pair of particles of the body is treated as constant. The rod can still move from one place to another, so its centre of mass need not remain fixed. During rotation, different points of the rod can have different velocities even though the body is rigid. Rigidity is about fixed geometry inside the body, not about equal velocity of all its points.

question: A rotating door is pushed near its handle rather than near its hinge mainly because
opt_a: the door's mass becomes smaller near the handle
opt_b: the push near the handle is internal to the door
opt_c: the hinge stops turning when pushed near it
opt_d: the larger distance gives a larger turning effect
explanation: A door is an extended rigid body that turns about an axis through its hinges. A push near the handle acts at a larger perpendicular distance from the hinge than a push near the hinge. For the same force direction, a larger distance from the axis gives a larger turning effect. This example shows why a rigid body cannot always be treated like a single particle. The position of application of force matters when rotation is involved.

question: Consider a long train moving along a straight track without turning. The motion of the train as a whole is best described as
opt_a: rotational motion about a fixed vertical axis only
opt_b: deformation of the train without displacement
opt_c: translational motion of an extended body
opt_d: pure spin about its own centre only
explanation: The train is an extended body because its size is not negligible in everyday description. If it moves straight ahead without changing orientation, its motion as a whole is translational. Different parts of the train shift forward along the track, and the body is not rotating about an axis. The fact that the train is large does not automatically make the motion rotational. Rotation is connected with change of orientation, whereas translation is connected with common shifting of the body.

question:
Study the table and choose the row that gives the most suitable example.
RowSituationMain idea shown
PA book sliding without turningTranslation
QA wheel spinning about a fixed axlePure translation
RA door rotating about its hingeParticle model only
SA rigid rod keeping fixed shapeDeformation
opt_d: Row S
explanation: A book sliding without turning is a good example of translational motion because its orientation remains unchanged. A wheel spinning about a fixed axle is rotational motion, not pure translation. A door rotating about its hinge is an extended-body rotation example, so it is not best described by the particle model alone. A rigid rod is assumed not to deform appreciably, so row S reverses the intended meaning. The table is testing whether the motion type is identified from orientation and body shape, not only from the object name.

question:
Assertion: Internal forces in a two-particle system can change the motion of individual particles.
Reason: Internal forces are forces that act between particles belonging to the same chosen system.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: Internal forces act between particles that are included in the same chosen system. Such forces can certainly change the velocities or paths of individual particles inside the system. For example, two interacting carts can push each other apart while both carts are included in one system. The Reason explains why those forces are called internal and also supports why they can act on the particles of the system. The important point is that internal forces do not change the acceleration of the centre of mass of the whole system when they cancel in action-reaction pairs.

question: A uniform circular ring has its centre of mass at its geometrical centre. That point is not occupied by material. This shows that the centre of mass
opt_a: must always lie outside every body
opt_b: must always lie inside solid material
opt_c: may lie where no material is present
opt_d: is meaningful only if a particle lies there
explanation: The centre of mass is a representative point determined by the distribution of mass. It need not coincide with an actual particle or a material point of the body. In a uniform ring, symmetry places the centre of mass at the centre, even though the material lies around the circumference. This is different from saying that the centre of mass is outside every body; for many uniform solid bodies it lies inside the material. The ring example is useful because it separates the idea of centre of mass from the idea of a physical piece of matter.

question: A body is made by joining a small heavy block to one end of a light rod. Compared with the geometrical midpoint of the rod, the centre of mass of the combined body will be shifted
opt_a: to a point unrelated to mass distribution
opt_c: exactly to the midpoint of the rod
opt_d: toward the empty end of the rod
explanation: The centre of mass depends on how mass is distributed, not only on the geometrical shape. A heavy block contributes more to the mass-weighted position than an equal-sized light portion. Therefore, attaching a heavy block to one end shifts the centre of mass toward that end. The geometrical midpoint is reliable only when the mass distribution has the required symmetry and uniformity. A visual midpoint can be misleading when one side carries much more mass.

question: The centre of mass is especially useful in system mechanics because it
opt_a: gives the position of the heaviest particle only
opt_b: removes the need to choose a system boundary
opt_c: represents translational motion of the system
opt_d: replaces every rotational motion by rest
explanation: For a system of particles, the centre of mass gives a compact description of the system's overall translational motion. Instead of tracking every particle separately for the motion of the whole system, one can often study the motion of this representative point. This does not remove rotational or internal motion; particles can still move relative to the centre of mass. It also does not necessarily coincide with the heaviest particle. The usefulness of the centre of mass comes from representing the weighted average motion of the system, not from ignoring all internal structure.

question: In a two-object system, one object is much heavier than the other. The centre of mass lies closer to the heavier object because
opt_a: it is always at the geometrical midpoint
opt_b: the lighter object has no effect at all
opt_c: mass weighting pulls it toward the heavier object
opt_d: only the heavier object has a position coordinate
explanation: Centre of mass is based on a mass-weighted average of positions. A heavier object contributes more strongly to that average than a lighter object at the same separation scale. The lighter object still affects the centre of mass, so it is not completely ignored. The midpoint occurs only in special cases such as two equal masses placed at the ends of a line segment. The heavier-side shift is a direct physical sign of mass weighting.

question:
Read the case and answer the question.
Two identical balls are fixed at the two ends of a light rod. A third identical ball is then fixed at the right end, so the right end now has twice as much mass as the left end.
How does the centre of mass shift after the third ball is added?
opt_a: It shifts toward the right end
opt_b: It shifts toward the left end
opt_c: It remains exactly at the rod's midpoint
opt_d: It disappears because the masses are discrete
explanation: Initially, two identical balls at the two ends have equal influence, so the centre of mass lies at the midpoint of the light rod. After adding another identical ball at the right end, the mass distribution is no longer symmetric. The right end has greater mass, so it pulls the mass-weighted average position toward itself. The masses being discrete does not make the centre of mass disappear; the centre of mass is well defined for discrete particles. The shift occurs because the right side now contributes more mass at its position.

question:
Consider the following statements about centre of mass.
I. It depends on the distribution of mass in the system.
II. It must always lie inside the material body.
III. It may represent the translational motion of the system.
opt_d: I and III only
explanation: Statement I is true because centre of mass is determined by how mass is spread in space. Statement III is also true because the centre of mass represents the translational motion of a system as a whole. Statement II is not generally true; the centre of mass may lie outside the material or at an empty point, as in a uniform ring. For uniform solid symmetric bodies it may lie inside, but that is not a universal rule. The safe idea is that centre of mass is a mass-distribution point, not necessarily a material point.

question: A non-uniform rod is thicker and heavier near its left end. Its geometrical midpoint and centre of mass are compared. The centre of mass is expected to be
opt_a: at the geometrical midpoint for every rod
opt_c: outside the rod on the right side in every case
opt_d: independent of the rod's density variation
explanation: A non-uniform rod does not have the same mass per unit length everywhere. If the left end is thicker and heavier, more mass is concentrated near that end. The centre of mass shifts toward the region where more mass is concentrated. The geometrical midpoint is the centre of length, not necessarily the centre of mass. Density variation matters because centre of mass follows mass distribution rather than shape alone.

question: In a uniform rectangular sheet, symmetry places the centre of mass at the intersection of the diagonals. If a small piece is removed from one corner, the new centre of mass shifts
opt_a: to the centre of the removed piece
opt_d: to a point that must be outside the sheet
explanation: Before removal, the uniform rectangular sheet has symmetric mass distribution, so its centre of mass is at the intersection of the diagonals. Removing a corner reduces mass from that side of the sheet. The remaining mass is relatively more concentrated away from the removed corner. Therefore, the centre of mass shifts away from the missing part. This is a qualitative application of the idea that removed mass can be treated as negative mass in composite-body problems.

question:
Match each situation with the most suitable centre-of-mass idea.
Column IColumn II
P. Uniform ring1. Centre of mass may lie at an empty point
Q. Two equal masses at the ends of a light rod2. Centre of mass lies at the midpoint
R. Non-uniform rod heavier at one end3. Centre of mass shifts toward greater mass concentration
S. System of many particles4. Centre of mass is found from mass-weighted positions
explanation: A uniform ring has its centre of mass at the centre, where there may be no material. Two equal masses at the ends of a light rod balance symmetrically, so their centre of mass lies at the midpoint. A non-uniform rod that is heavier at one end has its centre of mass shifted toward that end. For a general system of many particles, the centre of mass is based on mass-weighted positions. These matches separate symmetry, mass weighting, and empty-point location as different aspects of the same concept.

question: A statement says, "The centre of mass of a body is always the same as its geometrical centre." The best evaluation of this statement is that it is
opt_a: always true for every extended body
opt_b: true only with suitable symmetry and uniformity
opt_c: false because it never has a definite position
opt_d: true only for bodies moving with constant velocity
explanation: The geometrical centre is based on shape, while the centre of mass is based on mass distribution. If a body is uniform and symmetric, these two points often coincide. If the body is non-uniform or has missing parts, the centre of mass can shift away from the geometrical centre. The state of motion is not the deciding factor for the location of centre of mass in the body. The statement becomes reliable only after the mass distribution is checked, not from geometry alone.

question:
Use the graph description below.
Along a thin rod, the horizontal axis represents position from left to right and the vertical axis represents mass concentration. The graph is higher near the right end than near the left end.
What qualitative conclusion follows for the centre of mass of the rod?
opt_a: It must lie exactly at the left end.
opt_b: It shifts toward the right side of the rod.
opt_c: It is independent of mass concentration.
opt_d: It must lie outside the rod on the left side.
explanation: The graph says that more mass per unit length is concentrated near the right end of the rod. Centre of mass is a mass-weighted position, so regions with greater mass concentration influence it more strongly. For a uniform rod, symmetry would place the centre of mass at the midpoint. Here the higher concentration on the right breaks that symmetry and shifts the centre of mass rightward. The graph is qualitative, so it gives the direction of shift rather than an exact coordinate.

question: Four small beads are fixed on a light frame. Three beads of equal mass are placed near the left side, while one equal bead is placed far on the right side. Without numerical calculation, the centre of mass is best described as
opt_a: independent of the bead arrangement because the beads are equal
opt_b: always at the geometrical centre of the frame
opt_c: exactly at the position of the single right bead
opt_d: determined by both number of beads and their positions
explanation: Equal beads have equal mass, so each bead contributes equally in mass but not necessarily equally in position. The centre of mass depends on where all the beads are placed, not just on whether their masses are equal. Three beads on the left increase the left-side influence, while the far-right bead also matters because of its position. The final location cannot be decided from bead count alone unless the distances are specified. Centre of mass combines mass and position in one weighted description.

question: A hollow uniform spherical shell and a solid uniform sphere have the same outer centre. For each body considered separately, the centre of mass is at the common centre because
opt_a: mass is balanced symmetrically about the centre
opt_b: centre of mass must lie on the surface
opt_c: mass is concentrated only at the geometrical centre
opt_d: all particles of each body lie at the centre
explanation: In both a uniform spherical shell and a uniform solid sphere, mass is symmetrically distributed around the centre. For every small mass element in one direction, there is a corresponding mass element in the opposite direction that balances its position effect. This symmetry places the centre of mass at the centre. The shell may have no material at the centre, but that does not prevent the centre of mass from lying there. The deciding feature is balanced mass distribution, not the presence of material at the representative point.

question: For two particles of masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) placed at coordinates \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) on a straight line, the centre-of-mass coordinate is
explanation: For two particles on a line, the centre of mass is found by taking the mass-weighted average of their coordinates. The coordinate of each particle is multiplied by its mass because a larger mass has a stronger influence on the representative position. The denominator \(m_1+m_2\) is the total mass of the two-particle system. The simple average \(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\) is valid only when \(m_1=m_2\). The formula gives a coordinate, so its unit is the same as the unit of \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), usually \(\text{m}\).

question: Two particles of masses \(2\,\text{kg}\) and \(6\,\text{kg}\) are placed at \(x=0\,\text{m}\) and \(x=4\,\text{m}\), respectively. Find \(X_{\text{CM}}\).
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(x_1=0\,\text{m}\), \(m_2=6\,\text{kg}\), and \(x_2=4\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Centre-of-mass coordinate \(X_{\text{CM}}\).
\( \textbf{Useful relation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Reason for using it:} \) The particles lie on one straight line and their positions are given as coordinates on that line.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(2)(0)+(6)(4)}{2+6}\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Numerator:} \)
\[
(2)(0)+(6)(4)=24
\]
\( \textbf{Denominator:} \)
\[
2+6=8
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{24}{8}\,\text{m}=3\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Position check:} \) The result \(3\,\text{m}\) lies between \(0\,\text{m}\) and \(4\,\text{m}\), closer to the heavier \(6\,\text{kg}\) particle.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is at \(3\,\text{m}\) from the origin.

question: Two unequal masses are placed at the ends of a light rod of length \(L\). If \(m_1\) is at the left end and \(m_2\) is at the right end with \(m_2\gt m_1\), the centre of mass lies
opt_a: between the left end and the midpoint
opt_b: exactly at the midpoint of the rod
opt_c: between the midpoint and the right end
opt_d: outside the rod beyond the left end
explanation: For two positive masses placed at the ends of a line segment, the centre of mass must lie between them. It lies at the midpoint only when the two masses are equal. Since \(m_2\) is greater than \(m_1\), the right-end mass has a stronger pull on the mass-weighted average position. Therefore, the centre of mass shifts toward the right end. It does not go outside the rod for two positive endpoint masses because the weighted average of two endpoint coordinates stays between those coordinates.

question: A \(3\,\text{kg}\) particle is at \(x=-2\,\text{m}\), and a \(1\,\text{kg}\) particle is at \(x=6\,\text{m}\). The centre of mass of the two-particle system is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(m_1=3\,\text{kg}\), \(x_1=-2\,\text{m}\), \(m_2=1\,\text{kg}\), and \(x_2=6\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) \(X_{\text{CM}}\) for the two particles.
\( \textbf{Centre-of-mass formula:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution with signs:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(3)(-2)+(1)(6)}{3+1}\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Numerator calculation:} \)
\[
(3)(-2)+(1)(6)=-6+6=0
\]
\( \textbf{Denominator calculation:} \)
\[
3+1=4
\]
\( \textbf{Centre-of-mass coordinate:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{0}{4}\,\text{m}=0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Sign check:} \) The heavier particle is on the negative side, so the centre of mass is pulled leftward from the simple midpoint \(2\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is at the origin, \(0\,\text{m}\).

question: A two-particle system has \(m_1=m_2\). The centre of mass lies at the midpoint of the two particles because
opt_a: equal masses weight the two positions equally
opt_b: position has no role in locating the centre of mass
opt_c: the origin must be chosen at the midpoint
opt_d: the heavier particle pulls it to one side
explanation: When \(m_1=m_2\), the two coordinates contribute equally to the mass-weighted average. The formula becomes \(X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{mx_1+mx_2}{2m}\), which simplifies to \(X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\). This is exactly the coordinate of the midpoint between the two particles. The origin does not have to be at the midpoint; the formula gives the midpoint coordinate relative to whichever origin is chosen. The midpoint result is a consequence of equal masses, not a general rule for unequal masses.

Row S is wrong because shifting the origin changes the numerical coordinates, not the actual physical point in space. The coordinate value is origin-dependent, but the centre-of-mass location relative to the particles is not changed by relabelling the axis.

question: Two particles of masses \(m\) and \(3m\) are separated by a distance \(d\). Measured from the particle of mass \(m\), the distance of the centre of mass is
explanation:

\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Distance of the centre of mass from the mass \(m\).
\( \textbf{Formula:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m(0)+(3m)(d)}{m+3m}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{3md}{4m}
\]
\( \textbf{Cancel the common mass factor:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{3d}{4}
\]
\( \textbf{Location check:} \) The centre of mass is closer to \(3m\), so it should be more than \(\frac{d}{2}\) from the smaller mass.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is at a distance \(\frac{3d}{4}\) from the mass \(m\).

question:

Two particles are fixed on a horizontal line. Particle P has mass \(4m\) and particle Q has mass \(m\). The separation between them is \(10\,\text{cm}\).
The centre of mass is located

explanation:

\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Position of the centre of mass measured from P.
\( \textbf{Relation for two particles:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(4m)(0)+(m)(10)}{4m+m}\,\text{cm}
\]

\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{10m}{5m}\,\text{cm}
\]
\( \textbf{Distance from P:} \)
\[

\]
\( \textbf{Distance from Q:} \)
\[

\]
\( \textbf{Physical check:} \) Since P is four times heavier than Q, the centre of mass must be much closer to P.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is \(2\,\text{cm}\) from P and \(8\,\text{cm}\) from Q.

question: The relation \(X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}\) shows that the dimensions of \(X_{\text{CM}}\) are
explanation: In the numerator, each term such as \(m_1x_1\) has dimensions \([M][L]=[ML]\). The denominator \(m_1+m_2\) has dimension \([M]\). Dividing the numerator dimension \([ML]\) by the denominator dimension \([M]\) gives \([L]\). This is expected because \(X_{\text{CM}}\) is a coordinate or position. A centre-of-mass formula may contain mass, but the result is not a mass; it is a location.

question: A coordinate axis is shifted \(5\,\text{m}\) to the right. The coordinates of two fixed particles change, and the numerical value of \(X_{\text{CM}}\) also changes. What remains unchanged?
opt_a: The individual coordinate values of the particles
opt_d: The identity of the heavier particle
explanation: A change of origin changes the coordinate labels assigned to positions. Therefore, \(x_1\), \(x_2\), and the numerical coordinate \(X_{\text{CM}}\) may all change. However, the particles themselves have not moved, and their masses have not changed. The centre-of-mass point relative to those particles remains the same physical point. Coordinates are descriptions from a chosen origin, while the actual mass-weighted location is not moved by changing labels on the axis.

question: Two particles are placed at \(x=2\,\text{m}\) and \(x=8\,\text{m}\). Their centre of mass is found at \(x=6\,\text{m}\). What can be concluded about the masses?
opt_b: The two particles have equal masses
opt_d: Both particles must have zero mass
explanation: The midpoint of \(2\,\text{m}\) and \(8\,\text{m}\) is \(5\,\text{m}\). The given centre of mass is at \(6\,\text{m}\), which is closer to the particle at \(8\,\text{m}\) than to the particle at \(2\,\text{m}\). For two positive masses on a line, the centre of mass lies closer to the heavier mass. Therefore, the mass at \(8\,\text{m}\) must be larger than the mass at \(2\,\text{m}\). The conclusion comes from relative location, not from the coordinate values alone.

question:

The slope of this graph is
explanation:

\[

\]

X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1(0)+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]

\[

\]
\( \textbf{Physical meaning:} \) The slope is less than \(1\) because the centre of mass moves less than particle \(m_2\) when \(m_1\) stays fixed at the origin.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The slope is \(\frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}\).

question: Two particles of masses \(1\,\text{kg}\) and \(9\,\text{kg}\) are separated by \(1\,\text{m}\). A claim says, "The centre of mass is almost at the \(9\,\text{kg}\) particle, so the lighter particle can be ignored completely." The best response is that the claim is
opt_a: fully true because small masses never affect \(X_{\text{CM}}\)
opt_b: meaningless because two particles cannot have a centre of mass
opt_c: false because the centre of mass must be nearer the lighter mass
opt_d: misleading because the lighter mass still shifts \(X_{\text{CM}}\)
explanation: A much heavier mass strongly influences the centre-of-mass position, so the centre of mass will be close to the \(9\,\text{kg}\) particle. However, the \(1\,\text{kg}\) particle still contributes to the mass-weighted average. It cannot be ignored completely unless an approximation is being deliberately made and the required accuracy allows it. The centre of mass is not exactly at the heavier particle unless the lighter mass is zero or the separation is zero. This is a limiting-case idea: dominance by one mass is not the same as total absence of the other mass.

question: In the formula for two particles on a line, the blank is best completed as \(X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{\_\_\_\_}\).
explanation: The denominator of the centre-of-mass formula is the total mass of the system. For two particles, the total mass is \(m_1+m_2\). The numerator \(m_1x_1+m_2x_2\) is a mass-weighted position sum, so division by total mass converts it back into a position coordinate. Using \(m_1-m_2\) would fail when the masses are equal and would not represent averaging. The structure of the formula is weighted sum divided by total weight, where the weights are the masses.

question:
Assertion: For two positive masses on a line, the centre of mass lies between the two particle positions.
Reason: \(X_{\text{CM}}\) is a weighted average of the two coordinates with positive weights.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The assertion is true for two particles with positive masses placed at two different positions on a line. The centre-of-mass coordinate is formed by multiplying each coordinate by a positive mass and then dividing by the positive total mass. Such a weighted average must lie between the two coordinates. The reason directly explains why the centre of mass does not move outside the segment for this situation. Outside locations can occur for shapes such as rings because of geometry, but not for two positive point masses on a line segment.

question: A \(2\,\text{kg}\) particle is at \(x=1\,\text{m}\). Another particle of mass \(m\) is at \(x=5\,\text{m}\). If the centre of mass is at \(x=4\,\text{m}\), find \(m\).
explanation:
\( \textbf{Known values:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(x_1=1\,\text{m}\), \(m_2=m\), \(x_2=5\,\text{m}\), and \(X_{\text{CM}}=4\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Unknown mass \(m\).
\( \textbf{Centre-of-mass equation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitute the known values:} \)
\[
4=\frac{(2)(1)+m(5)}{2+m}
\]
\( \textbf{Clear the denominator:} \)
\[
4(2+m)=2+5m
\]
\( \textbf{Expand the left side:} \)
\[
8+4m=2+5m
\]
\( \textbf{Collect terms:} \)
\[
8-2=5m-4m
\]
\( \textbf{Solve for the unknown mass:} \)
\[
m=6\,\text{kg}
\]
\( \textbf{Reasonableness check:} \) The centre of mass at \(4\,\text{m}\) is closer to \(5\,\text{m}\), so the unknown mass should be greater than \(2\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The second particle has mass \(6\,\text{kg}\).

question: A two-particle system has masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) at positions \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). If both masses are doubled while their positions remain unchanged, \(X_{\text{CM}}\) will
opt_d: become half
explanation: The centre-of-mass coordinate depends on the ratio of the weighted position sum to the total mass. If both masses are doubled, the numerator \(m_1x_1+m_2x_2\) is doubled. The denominator \(m_1+m_2\) is also doubled. These two factors cancel, leaving the same value of \(X_{\text{CM}}\). Scaling all masses by the same factor does not change the mass distribution ratio, so the centre-of-mass position remains unchanged.

question: A \(5\,\text{kg}\) particle is at \(x=0\,\text{m}\), and a \(1\,\text{kg}\) particle is at \(x=12\,\text{m}\). If only the \(1\,\text{kg}\) particle is moved to \(x=18\,\text{m}\), the centre of mass shifts by
opt_d: \(1.0\,\text{m}\) to the right
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial setup:} \) \(m_1=5\,\text{kg}\) at \(0\,\text{m}\), and \(m_2=1\,\text{kg}\) at \(12\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Initial centre of mass:} \)
\[
X_i=\frac{(5)(0)+(1)(12)}{5+1}\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Initial value:} \)
\[
X_i=\frac{12}{6}\,\text{m}=2\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final setup:} \) The \(1\,\text{kg}\) particle moves to \(18\,\text{m}\), while the \(5\,\text{kg}\) particle remains at \(0\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final centre of mass:} \)
\[
X_f=\frac{(5)(0)+(1)(18)}{5+1}\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final value:} \)
\[
X_f=\frac{18}{6}\,\text{m}=3\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Shift:} \)
\[
X_f-X_i=3\,\text{m}-2\,\text{m}=1\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction:} \) The shift is positive, so it is to the right.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass shifts by \(1.0\,\text{m}\) to the right.

question: For a system of many particles, the vector expression for the centre of mass is
opt_d: \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\sum \vec{r}_i}{\sum m_i}\)
explanation: For many particles, the centre of mass is found by adding the mass-weighted position vectors of all particles. The term \(m_i\vec{r}_i\) represents the contribution of the \(i^{\text{th}}\) particle to the weighted position sum. Dividing by the total mass \(M=\sum m_i\) converts this weighted sum into a position vector. The vector form is useful because it works in one, two, or three dimensions. The expression is not a simple average of position vectors unless all particles have equal masses.

question: In the component method for a many-particle system, \(X_{\text{CM}}\) is found using
opt_b: only the particles lying on the \(x\)-axis
opt_d: the simple average of all distances from the origin
explanation: The component method treats the centre-of-mass vector component by component. The \(x\)-coordinate of the centre of mass is found from all particle \(x\)-coordinates, each weighted by the corresponding mass. The formula is \(X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i}\). Particles need not lie on the \(x\)-axis to contribute to \(X_{\text{CM}}\); only their \(x\)-coordinates are used for that component. The same idea applies separately to \(Y_{\text{CM}}\) and \(Z_{\text{CM}}\).

question: Three particles of masses \(1\,\text{kg}\), \(2\,\text{kg}\), and \(3\,\text{kg}\) are placed at \(x=0\,\text{m}\), \(x=3\,\text{m}\), and \(x=6\,\text{m}\), respectively. Find \(X_{\text{CM}}\).
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(m_1=1\,\text{kg}\), \(x_1=0\,\text{m}\), \(m_2=2\,\text{kg}\), \(x_2=3\,\text{m}\), \(m_3=3\,\text{kg}\), and \(x_3=6\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) \(X_{\text{CM}}\) of the three-particle system.
\( \textbf{Formula for many particles on a line:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(1)(0)+(2)(3)+(3)(6)}{1+2+3}\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Numerator:} \)
\[
(1)(0)+(2)(3)+(3)(6)=0+6+18=24
\]
\( \textbf{Denominator:} \)
\[
1+2+3=6
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{24}{6}\,\text{m}=4\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Location check:} \) The result is to the right of the simple coordinate average \(3\,\text{m}\) because the heavier mass is at \(6\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is at \(4\,\text{m}\).

question: For particles in a plane, the centre-of-mass coordinates are calculated separately as \(X_{\text{CM}}\) and \(Y_{\text{CM}}\). This works because
opt_a: mass is split into separate \(x\)- and \(y\)-components
opt_b: vector addition resolves into rectangular components
opt_c: only particles lying on the coordinate axes are counted
opt_d: the centre of mass is always located at the origin
explanation: The vector formula \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum m_i\vec{r}_i\) contains position vectors. Each position vector can be resolved into \(x\)- and \(y\)-components in a plane. Therefore, the same weighted-average idea can be applied separately to the \(x\)-coordinates and the \(y\)-coordinates. Mass itself is scalar and does not split into components; it only weights the position components. The component method is just the vector formula written in a calculation-friendly form.

question: Three particles are placed at \(P(0,0)\), \(Q(4\,\text{m},0)\), and \(R(0,3\,\text{m})\), each of mass \(2\,\text{kg}\). The centre of mass is
opt_d: \(\left(\frac{8}{3}\,\text{m},2\,\text{m}\right)\)
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) The three masses are equal, each \(2\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Coordinates:} \) \(P(0,0)\), \(Q(4\,\text{m},0)\), and \(R(0,3\,\text{m})\).
\( \textbf{Useful simplification:} \) For equal masses, each coordinate of the centre of mass becomes the simple average of the corresponding coordinates.
\( \textbf{x-coordinate:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{0+4+0}{3}\,\text{m}=\frac{4}{3}\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{y-coordinate:} \)
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=\frac{0+0+3}{3}\,\text{m}=1\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Coordinate pair:} \)
\[
\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}\equiv \left(\frac{4}{3}\,\text{m},1\,\text{m}\right)
\]
\( \textbf{Reasonableness check:} \) The point lies inside the triangular region formed by the three equal masses.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is \(\left(\frac{4}{3}\,\text{m},1\,\text{m}\right)\).

question:
Consider the following statements for a many-particle system.
I. \(M=\sum m_i\) is the total mass of the chosen system.
II. \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}\) has the same unit as \(\vec{r}_i\).
III. The largest mass alone always gives the exact centre-of-mass position.
opt_d: II and III only
explanation: Statement I is true because the total mass is the sum of the masses of all particles included in the chosen system. Statement II is also true because \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}\) is a position vector, so it has the same unit as \(\vec{r}_i\), usually \(\text{m}\). Statement III is not generally true because every mass contributes to the weighted average. A very large mass may dominate the centre-of-mass location, but smaller masses still affect the exact position. The centre of mass is found from the whole mass distribution, not from one particle alone.

question: A system has two particles of mass \(m\) at \(x=-a\) and \(x=+a\), and a third particle of mass \(2m\) at \(x=0\). Its centre of mass is
explanation:

question: A claim says, "For several particles, \(X_{\text{CM}}\) can be found by averaging only the extreme left and extreme right coordinates." This method is reliable only when
opt_a: the origin is placed at the leftmost particle
opt_b: the centre of mass is required in two dimensions
opt_c: the masses and intermediate positions do not affect the weighted average
opt_d: all particles have equal masses and are located only at the two extremes
explanation: For a general many-particle system, all particles included in the system contribute to \(X_{\text{CM}}\). Averaging only the extreme coordinates ignores masses and ignores any particles between the extremes. That can accidentally work in very special symmetric situations, but it is not the general method. The correct relation is \(X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i}\). The centre of mass depends on the full weighted distribution, not only on the outermost positions.

question: Four particles are placed on a line: \(2\,\text{kg}\) at \(x=0\,\text{m}\), \(1\,\text{kg}\) at \(x=2\,\text{m}\), \(3\,\text{kg}\) at \(x=4\,\text{m}\), and \(2\,\text{kg}\) at \(x=8\,\text{m}\). The centre of mass is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) The particles have masses \(2\,\text{kg}\), \(1\,\text{kg}\), \(3\,\text{kg}\), and \(2\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Positions:} \) Their coordinates are \(0\,\text{m}\), \(2\,\text{m}\), \(4\,\text{m}\), and \(8\,\text{m}\), respectively.

\]

\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)

X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{30}{8}\,\text{m}=3.75\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Check:} \) The value lies between \(0\,\text{m}\) and \(8\,\text{m}\), as expected for positive masses on a line.

question:

The expression \(\sum m_ix_i\) is the weighted sum needed for the \(x\)-coordinate of the centre of mass. Similarly, \(\sum m_iy_i\) is the weighted sum needed for the \(y\)-coordinate. The symbol \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}\) represents the final position vector of the centre of mass. The matching keeps scalar total mass separate from vector or component position information.

question: A set of three particles lies in the \(xy\)-plane. Their data are \(m_1=1\,\text{kg}\) at \((0,0)\), \(m_2=1\,\text{kg}\) at \((6\,\text{m},0)\), and \(m_3=2\,\text{kg}\) at \((0,4\,\text{m})\). Find the centre of mass.
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(m_1=1\,\text{kg}\), \(m_2=1\,\text{kg}\), and \(m_3=2\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Coordinates:} \) \((0,0)\), \((6\,\text{m},0)\), and \((0,4\,\text{m})\).
\( \textbf{Total mass:} \)
\[
M=1+1+2=4\,\text{kg}
\]
\( \textbf{x-coordinate relation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\sum m_ix_i}{M}
\]
\( \textbf{x-coordinate calculation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(1)(0)+(1)(6)+(2)(0)}{4}\,\text{m}=\frac{6}{4}\,\text{m}=1.5\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{y-coordinate relation:} \)
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\sum m_iy_i}{M}
\]
\( \textbf{y-coordinate calculation:} \)
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(1)(0)+(1)(0)+(2)(4)}{4}\,\text{m}=\frac{8}{4}\,\text{m}=2.0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is \((1.5\,\text{m},2.0\,\text{m})\).

question: In the vector formula \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum m_i\vec{r}_i\), shifting every particle by the same displacement vector \(\vec{a}\) changes the centre-of-mass position vector by
opt_d: \(M\vec{a}\)
explanation: If every particle is shifted by the same vector \(\vec{a}\), each position vector changes from \(\vec{r}_i\) to \(\vec{r}_i+\vec{a}\). The new centre-of-mass vector is \(\vec{R}'_{\text{CM}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum m_i(\vec{r}_i+\vec{a})\). This becomes \(\frac{1}{M}\sum m_i\vec{r}_i+\frac{1}{M}\sum m_i\vec{a}\). Since \(\sum m_i=M\), the second term becomes \(\vec{a}\). A common translation of the whole system translates the centre of mass by the same vector.

question: A data-processing error replaces \(\sum m_ix_i\) by \(\sum m_i+\sum x_i\) while finding \(X_{\text{CM}}\). The result is physically unacceptable mainly because
opt_a: masses and positions can always be added directly
opt_b: \(\sum m_i+\sum x_i\) adds quantities of different dimensions
opt_c: centre of mass has no unit
opt_d: the numerator of \(X_{\text{CM}}\) should contain only coordinates
explanation: The numerator in \(X_{\text{CM}}\) must be a sum of terms like \(m_ix_i\), each having dimension \([ML]\). The expression \(\sum m_i+\sum x_i\) attempts to add mass and length terms directly. Such addition is dimensionally invalid because quantities of different dimensions cannot be added. The centre-of-mass coordinate must finally have dimension \([L]\). Dimensional consistency helps detect formula errors before any numerical calculation is trusted.

question:
Read the case below and answer the question.
A light frame carries three small masses. One mass \(m\) is fixed at the origin, another mass \(m\) is fixed at \((2a,0)\), and a third mass \(2m\) is fixed at \((0,2a)\).
The position of the centre of mass is
opt_d: \(\left(a,\frac{a}{2}\right)\)
explanation:
\( \textbf{Mass-position data:} \) The masses are \(m\) at \((0,0)\), \(m\) at \((2a,0)\), and \(2m\) at \((0,2a)\).
\( \textbf{Total mass:} \)
\[
M=m+m+2m=4m
\]
\( \textbf{x-coordinate of centre of mass:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m(0)+m(2a)+2m(0)}{4m}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplify the x-coordinate expression:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{2ma}{4m}=\frac{a}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{y-coordinate of centre of mass:} \)
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m(0)+m(0)+2m(2a)}{4m}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplify the y-coordinate expression:} \)
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=\frac{4ma}{4m}=a
\]
\( \textbf{Coordinate pair:} \)
\[
\left(X_{\text{CM}},Y_{\text{CM}}\right)=\left(\frac{a}{2},a\right)
\]
\( \textbf{Location check:} \) The \(2m\) mass at \((0,2a)\) pulls the centre of mass upward more strongly than the single mass at \((2a,0)\) pulls it rightward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is \(\left(\frac{a}{2},a\right)\).

question: For particles distributed in three-dimensional space, the \(z\)-coordinate of the centre of mass is written as
opt_d: \(Z_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\sum m_iz_i}{\sum m_i}\)
explanation: The component method applies the same weighted-average rule separately along each coordinate direction. For the \(z\)-coordinate, each particle contributes \(m_iz_i\) to the weighted sum. The denominator must be the total mass \(\sum m_i\). The expression \(\sum m_iz_i\) alone has dimension \([ML]\), so it cannot be a coordinate by itself. Dividing by total mass gives a result with dimension \([L]\), matching the meaning of \(Z_{\text{CM}}\).

question: Three particles have masses \(1\,\text{kg}\), \(2\,\text{kg}\), and \(3\,\text{kg}\) at positions \((0,0,0)\), \((3\,\text{m},0,0)\), and \((0,6\,\text{m},0)\), respectively. The centre of mass is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(m_1=1\,\text{kg}\), \(m_2=2\,\text{kg}\), and \(m_3=3\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Position data:} \) \((0,0,0)\), \((3\,\text{m},0,0)\), and \((0,6\,\text{m},0)\).
\( \textbf{Total mass:} \)
\[
M=1+2+3=6\,\text{kg}
\]
\( \textbf{x-coordinate:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(1)(0)+(2)(3)+(3)(0)}{6}\,\text{m}
\]
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{6}{6}\,\text{m}=1\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{y-coordinate:} \)
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(1)(0)+(2)(0)+(3)(6)}{6}\,\text{m}
\]
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=\frac{18}{6}\,\text{m}=3\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{z-coordinate:} \) All particles have \(z=0\), so \(Z_{\text{CM}}=0\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is \((1\,\text{m},3\,\text{m},0)\).

question:
Consider the following statements about \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum m_i\vec{r}_i\).
I. The formula uses the position vector of every particle in the chosen system.
II. The total mass \(M\) is a scalar.
III. The formula is valid only when all particles lie on a straight line.
opt_d: I, II, and III
explanation: Statement I is true because the summation includes all particles that belong to the chosen system. Statement II is true because total mass has magnitude only and is not a vector. Statement III is false because the vector formula works in one, two, or three dimensions. When particles lie on a line, the same formula simply reduces to a one-coordinate form. The vector notation is introduced precisely to handle general spatial distributions without changing the basic weighted-average idea.

question:
A table of values is prepared for finding \(X_{\text{CM}}\) of several particles.
RowQuantity enteredUse in calculation
P\(m_i\)Add to get total mass
Q\(x_i\)Use with \(m_i\) to form \(m_ix_i\)
R\(m_ix_i\)Add to get weighted position sum
S\(\sum x_i\)Divide by \(\sum m_i\) for unequal masses
The row that contains an unsuitable method is
opt_d: Row P
explanation: Rows P, Q, and R follow the correct setup for a centre-of-mass calculation. The total mass is found from \(\sum m_i\), and the weighted position sum is found from \(\sum m_ix_i\). Row S is unsuitable for unequal masses because it averages coordinates without applying mass weights. Dividing \(\sum x_i\) by \(\sum m_i\) is also dimensionally wrong, since the numerator has dimension \([L]\) and the denominator has dimension \([M]\). For unequal masses, the required numerator is \(\sum m_ix_i\), not \(\sum x_i\).

question: Particles of masses \(2\,\text{kg}\) and \(3\,\text{kg}\) are placed at \(x=1\,\text{m}\) and \(x=4\,\text{m}\). A third particle of mass \(5\,\text{kg}\) is placed at \(x=a\). If the centre of mass is at \(x=3\,\text{m}\), the value of \(a\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Known values:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(x_1=1\,\text{m}\), \(m_2=3\,\text{kg}\), \(x_2=4\,\text{m}\), \(m_3=5\,\text{kg}\), and \(X_{\text{CM}}=3\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Unknown coordinate:} \) \(x_3=a\).
\( \textbf{Centre-of-mass relation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2+m_3x_3}{m_1+m_2+m_3}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
3=\frac{(2)(1)+(3)(4)+(5)(a)}{2+3+5}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplify denominator:} \)
\[
2+3+5=10
\]
\( \textbf{Clear denominator:} \)
\[
30=2+12+5a
\]
\( \textbf{Collect terms:} \)
\[
30=14+5a
\]
\[
5a=16
\]
\( \textbf{Solve:} \)
\[
a=3.2\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The third particle must be placed at \(3.2\,\text{m}\).

question:
Use the graph description below.
Two fixed particles are at \(x=0\) and \(x=L\). The mass at \(x=0\) is kept fixed, while the mass at \(x=L\) is gradually increased from a small value to a very large value.
As the mass at \(x=L\) increases, \(X_{\text{CM}}\)
opt_b: moves toward \(x=0\) and then becomes negative
opt_c: moves toward \(x=L\) but remains between \(0\) and \(L\)
opt_d: stays exactly at \(\frac{L}{2}\) for all masses
explanation: For two positive masses at \(0\) and \(L\), the centre-of-mass coordinate is a weighted average of the two endpoint coordinates. Increasing the mass at \(x=L\) increases the weight of the coordinate \(L\) in that average. Therefore, the centre of mass shifts toward \(x=L\). It does not go beyond \(L\) because both masses are positive and the weighted average of two endpoints remains between them. In the limiting case of a very large mass at \(L\), the centre of mass comes very close to \(L\) without needing to cross it.

question: For a continuous body, the centre-of-mass formula is obtained from the discrete-particle formula by replacing
opt_d: \(dm\) by \(\frac{1}{M}\) in the integral
explanation: A continuous body can be imagined as being made of many very small mass elements \(dm\). The discrete weighted sum \(\sum m_i\vec{r}_i\) then becomes the integral \(\int \vec{r}\,dm\). The total mass remains \(M=\int dm\). Thus, the centre of mass is written as \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}=\frac{1}{M}\int \vec{r}\,dm\). The change from summation to integration reflects continuous mass distribution, not a change in the physical meaning of centre of mass.

question: The expression \(\vec{R}_{\text{CM}}=\frac{1}{M}\int \vec{r}\,dm\) is mainly used when the mass distribution is
opt_a: concentrated at a single point particle
opt_b: given as a small listed set of particles
opt_d: kept entirely at the chosen origin
explanation: The integral form is used when a body is not conveniently described as a small list of separate particles. Examples include rods, plates, discs, and solid bodies with mass spread continuously. The small mass element \(dm\) represents a tiny part of the body at position \(\vec{r}\). Adding all such contributions through an integral gives the weighted position of the entire body. For a few listed particles, the summation formula is usually the more direct method.

question:
Match the type of continuous distribution with a suitable mass element idea.
Column IColumn II
P. Thin wire1. Line mass element
Q. Thin lamina2. Area mass element
R. Solid body3. Volume mass element
S. Whole body mass4. \(M=\int dm\)
explanation: A thin wire is naturally treated as a line distribution because its mass is spread mainly along length. A thin lamina is treated as an area distribution because its thickness is negligible compared with its surface dimensions. A solid body requires a volume distribution when its full three-dimensional spread matters. The total mass of any continuous body can be written as \(M=\int dm\). These descriptions choose the form of \(dm\), while the centre-of-mass idea remains a mass-weighted position average.

question: For a uniform thin rod along the \(x\)-axis, the small mass element may be written as \(dm=\lambda\,dx\), where \(\lambda\) is constant. This helps because
opt_a: it removes the need to locate the rod
opt_b: it relates each mass element to a length element
opt_c: it makes the total mass of the rod equal to zero
opt_d: it changes the rod into a point particle
explanation: For a line distribution, \(dm\) represents the mass of a small length element. If the rod is uniform, the mass per unit length \(\lambda\) is constant, so \(dm=\lambda\,dx\). This converts the centre-of-mass integral into an integral over position \(x\). The rod is still an extended continuous body; it is not being changed into a point particle. Uniformity simplifies the integral because \(\lambda\) can be treated as constant.

question: A uniform rod extends from \(x=0\) to \(x=L\). Using \(\lambda=\frac{M}{L}\), the centre of mass is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Body:} \) A uniform rod extends from \(x=0\) to \(x=L\).
\( \textbf{Mass element:} \) For a uniform rod, \(dm=\lambda\,dx\), where \(\lambda=\frac{M}{L}\).
\( \textbf{Centre-of-mass formula:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{1}{M}\int x\,dm
\]
\( \textbf{Substitute the mass element:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{1}{M}\int_0^L x\lambda\,dx
\]
\( \textbf{Take the constant linear density outside:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\lambda}{M}\int_0^L x\,dx
\]
\( \textbf{Evaluate the integral:} \)
\[
\int_0^L x\,dx=\frac{L^2}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Use the uniform-rod density relation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{1}{M}\left(\frac{M}{L}\right)\frac{L^2}{2}
\]
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{L}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass lies at the midpoint, \(\frac{L}{2}\), measured from \(x=0\).

question: A continuous body has non-uniform density. In finding its centre of mass, one must be careful because
opt_a: the body must be treated as massless
opt_b: equal lengths or areas may contain unequal masses
opt_c: the coordinate system cannot be chosen
opt_d: the centre-of-mass formula becomes meaningless for non-uniform density
explanation: Non-uniform density means mass is not spread equally throughout the body. Two equal-sized small parts of the body may contain different amounts of mass. Since centre of mass is a mass-weighted position, the denser regions influence it more strongly. The formula remains meaningful, but \(dm\) must represent the actual local mass element. Treating the body as uniform when it is not uniform can place the centre of mass at a wrong position.

question: In the integral \(\int \vec{r}\,dm\), the vector \(\vec{r}\) represents
opt_a: the position vector of each small mass element
opt_b: the radius measured only from the outer surface
opt_c: the angular velocity vector of the body
opt_d: the torque vector on each mass element
explanation: In a continuous body, the integral adds contributions from many small mass elements. The vector \(\vec{r}\) gives the position of the particular element \(dm\) relative to the chosen origin. The product \(\vec{r}\,dm\) is therefore the mass-weighted position contribution of that element. As the integration covers the whole body, all such contributions are included. The symbol \(\vec{r}\) in this formula is a position vector, not an angular velocity or torque.

question: A thin plate has uniform surface mass density \(\sigma\). For a small area element \(dA\), the mass element is
opt_d: \(dm=\sigma\,dA\)
explanation: Surface mass density \(\sigma\) means mass per unit area. Therefore, a small area element \(dA\) contains mass \(dm=\sigma\,dA\) when \(\sigma\) is uniform. This is the area-distribution analogue of \(dm=\lambda\,dx\) for a thin wire. The product \(\sigma\,dA\) has the dimension of mass because \(\sigma\) has unit \(\text{kg m}^{-2}\) and \(dA\) has unit \(\text{m}^2\). This relation lets an area integral be used for the centre of mass of a lamina.

question: A compact way to describe the transition from a discrete system to a continuous body is
opt_a: total mass is replaced by position
opt_b: centre of mass must shift to the origin
opt_d: mass weighting is no longer needed in the formula
explanation: A discrete system is described by separate particles with masses \(m_i\) at positions \(\vec{r}_i\). A continuous body is treated as a collection of infinitesimal mass elements \(dm\), each with its own position \(\vec{r}\). The weighted sum \(\sum m_i\vec{r}_i\) becomes the integral \(\int \vec{r}\,dm\). Mass weighting remains the central idea in both descriptions. The mathematical form changes because the mass is continuously spread rather than listed as separate particles.

question: A uniform wire is bent into a shape but its mass per unit length remains constant everywhere. While setting up its centre-of-mass calculation, the most important local element is
opt_a: the total mass placed at every point of the wire
opt_d: a small angle element \(d\theta\) with no mass relation possible
explanation: A wire is a line distribution, even if it is bent into a curved shape. The natural small element is a small length \(dl\) along the wire. If the wire is uniform, its mass per unit length \(\lambda\) is constant, so the small mass element is \(dm=\lambda\,dl\). The position vector of each small element must still be included in \(\int \vec{r}\,dm\). The bending of the wire changes the positions of the elements, but it does not change the basic line-distribution mass element.

question: A uniform thin rod of length \(L\) is placed along a straight line. By symmetry, its centre of mass is located
opt_a: at a distance \(\frac{L}{4}\) from one end
opt_b: at one end of the rod
opt_d: at the midpoint of the rod
explanation: A uniform rod has equal mass distribution on both sides of its midpoint. For every small element at a distance \(x\) to one side of the midpoint, there is an equal mass element at the same distance on the other side. These opposite contributions balance in the mass-weighted average. Therefore, the centre of mass lies at the midpoint. This conclusion depends on uniformity; a non-uniform rod need not have its centre of mass at the geometrical midpoint.

question: A uniform circular ring is lying in a plane. Its centre of mass is at the geometrical centre because
opt_a: the ring has no mass along its circumference
opt_b: centre of mass must lie inside the material
opt_c: all its mass is concentrated at the centre
opt_d: opposite mass elements balance one another
explanation: A uniform circular ring has rotational symmetry about its centre. For each small mass element on the ring, an equal mass element lies diametrically opposite to it. Their position contributions cancel pairwise about the centre. The centre of mass is therefore at the geometrical centre of the ring. The centre is not occupied by the material of the ring, so this example also shows that the centre of mass need not be a material point.

question:
Study the table and choose the row with the suitable centre-of-mass location for a uniform body.
RowUniform bodyCentre of mass
PThin rodMidpoint
QCircular ringAny point on circumference
RCircular discAny point on rim
SRectangular laminaOne corner
opt_d: Row S
explanation: A uniform thin rod has its centre of mass at its midpoint because its mass is symmetrically distributed along its length. A uniform circular ring has its centre of mass at its centre, not at an arbitrary point on the circumference. A uniform circular disc also has its centre of mass at its centre, not on the rim. A uniform rectangular lamina has its centre of mass at the intersection of its diagonals, not at a corner. Symmetry gives reliable results only when the body is uniform and the stated symmetry is actually present.

question: The centre of mass of a uniform rectangular lamina lies at
opt_b: the midpoint of one side only
opt_c: the corner nearest to the longer side
opt_d: a point outside the lamina in every case
explanation: A uniform rectangular lamina has equal mass distribution around the intersection of its diagonals. The vertical line through this point divides the rectangle into two equal-mass halves, and the horizontal line through it also divides the rectangle into two equal-mass halves. These two symmetry balances meet at the same point. Hence the centre of mass lies at the intersection of the diagonals. This result would not remain valid if a corner were cut away or if the lamina had non-uniform density.

question:
Consider the following statements about centre of mass by symmetry.
I. A uniform solid sphere has its centre of mass at its centre.
II. A uniform circular disc has its centre of mass at its centre.
III. A uniform ring cannot have its centre of mass at an empty point.
opt_d: I and II only
explanation: Statement I is true because a uniform solid sphere has complete symmetry about its centre. Statement II is true because a uniform disc has circular symmetry in its plane, placing the centre of mass at its geometrical centre. Statement III is false because a uniform ring has its centre of mass at the centre of the ring, where no material may be present. Symmetry decides the centre-of-mass location from balanced mass distribution, not from the requirement that material must exist at that point. The ring is the clearest reminder that centre of mass is a representative point.

question: A uniform square lamina is folded conceptually along one diagonal into two equal triangular halves. This observation supports that its centre of mass lies
opt_a: only at one vertex of the square
opt_d: at every point on the boundary
explanation: If a uniform square is divided by a diagonal, the two triangular halves have equal area and equal mass. The centre of mass of the whole square must lie on the line of symmetry that balances these two halves. One diagonal alone tells us that the centre of mass lies somewhere on that diagonal. The other diagonal gives another symmetry line, and the intersection of the two diagonals fixes the exact centre. A single symmetry line narrows the location, while two independent symmetry lines locate it exactly.

question: A uniform circular disc has a small circular hole cut symmetrically at its centre. The remaining body is a uniform ring-like lamina. Its centre of mass is
opt_c: at the edge of the hole
opt_d: outside the lamina
explanation: Removing a central circular hole from a uniform disc preserves circular symmetry about the same centre. For every remaining mass element, an equal mass element still exists at the opposite position. The missing part is also symmetric about the centre, so it does not favour any particular direction. Therefore, the centre of mass of the remaining ring-like lamina remains at the common centre. The absence of material at the centre does not prevent the centre of mass from being located there.

question: A square lamina is uniform, but a small identical square is removed from its upper-right corner. Compared with the original centre, the new centre of mass shifts
opt_a: nowhere because the outer shape was originally symmetric
opt_d: away from the upper-right corner
explanation: The original uniform square has its centre of mass at its geometrical centre due to symmetry. Removing a small square from the upper-right corner removes mass from that side of the lamina. The remaining mass is then relatively more concentrated toward the lower-left side. Hence the centre of mass shifts away from the removed corner. Original symmetry cannot be used after the removal because the mass distribution of the remaining body is no longer symmetric in the same way.

question:
Assertion: The centre of mass of a uniform ring lies at its geometrical centre.
Reason: The material of a uniform ring is concentrated at the geometrical centre.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The assertion is true because a uniform ring has complete symmetry about its centre. Equal mass elements on opposite sides of the centre balance their position contributions. The reason is false because the material of a ring is not concentrated at the centre; it is distributed around the circumference. The centre of mass lies at the centre because of symmetry, not because material is physically present there. This distinction prevents the mistaken idea that centre of mass must always be an occupied point.

question: A uniform semicircular wire has less symmetry than a complete circular ring. Its centre of mass is expected to lie
opt_a: at the centre of the original full circle
opt_b: at either end of the semicircular wire
opt_c: on the symmetry axis of the semicircle
opt_d: at every point of the circular arc
explanation: A semicircular wire still has one line of symmetry passing through the midpoint of the arc and the centre of the original circle. Mass elements on the left and right sides of this symmetry line balance each other. Therefore, the centre of mass must lie on this symmetry axis. However, the upper and lower parts are not symmetrically distributed like a complete ring, so it need not lie at the centre of the original circle. Symmetry can restrict the possible line of location even when it does not give the exact point immediately.

question: For a composite body made of simple parts, the centre of mass can often be found by
opt_a: using only the outermost dimensions of the body
opt_b: treating each part as concentrated at its centre of mass
opt_c: placing it at the geometrical centre in every case
opt_d: ignoring the masses of larger parts of the composite body
explanation: A composite body can be divided into simpler parts whose individual centres of mass are known. For centre-of-mass calculation, each part may be replaced by a point mass located at its own centre of mass. The mass of that part is then used in the weighted-average formula. This method works because centre of mass depends on total mass and mass-weighted position, not on the detailed shape after each part's centre of mass is known. The geometrical centre is safe only for uniform symmetric bodies, not for every composite body.

question: A uniform rod of length \(3L\) is made by joining two uniform rods along the same line: one has length \(L\) and mass \(m\), and the other has length \(2L\) and mass \(2m\). The rods are joined end to end, with the shorter rod on the left. Measured from the left end, the centre of mass is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Parts of the body:} \) The shorter rod has mass \(m\) and length \(L\); the longer rod has mass \(2m\) and length \(2L\).
\( \textbf{Choose origin:} \) Take the left end of the shorter rod as \(x=0\).
\( \textbf{Centre of shorter rod:} \)
\[
x_1=\frac{L}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Centre of longer rod:} \) The longer rod extends from \(x=L\) to \(x=3L\), so its centre is
\[
x_2=2L
\]
\( \textbf{Composite centre-of-mass formula:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)+2m(2L)}{m+2m}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplify numerator:} \)
\[
\frac{mL}{2}+4mL=\frac{9mL}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Divide by total mass:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\frac{9mL}{2}}{3m}=\frac{3L}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Option check:} \) The value \(\frac{3L}{2}\) lies between \(L\) and \(2L\), closer to the longer rod because that rod has the greater mass.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is at \(\frac{3L}{2}\) from the left end.
